issues.subcategory: The abstract’s 1–2 second framing does not match the reported timing
issues.description: The abstract’s 1–2 second framing does not match the reported timing: “Within this timeframe” points back to “just 1 or 2 seconds ago”, but the experiments use probe delays including 0.5/0.75 s and 3 s, with responses often occurring after a later second display. The abstract should not imply that the decisive change is measured wholly inside a 1–2 s window. A safer summary would refer to “brief delays of up to a few seconds” and distinguish probe timing from response timing.
issues.quote: However, it is generally assumed that short-term memory for percepts formed just 1 or 2 seconds ago accurately represents the percepts as they were at the time of perception. Here 4 experiments consistently show that within this timeframe, participants go from reliably reporting what was there (perceptual inference accurately reflecting the bottom-up input), to erroneously but with high confidence reporting what they expected to be there (memory report strongly influenced by top-down expectations).

issues.subcategory: Misleading claim about initial reliability
issues.description: Misleading claim about initial reliability: The Abstract's temporal contrast seems somewhat too categorical. At the earliest measured delays (500–750 ms after offset), high-confidence pseudo-to-real illusions are already substantial, although they increase with delay/interference. The evidence supports a memory-dependent increase, but not a clean transition from initially unbiased reports to later expectation-driven errors.
issues.quote: Here 4 experiments consistently show that within this timeframe, participants go from reliably reporting what was there (perceptual inference accurately reflecting the bottom-up input), to erroneously but with high confidence reporting what they expected to be there (memory report strongly influenced by top-down expectations).

issues.subcategory: Abstract inference about visual similarity feels too strong
issues.description: Abstract inference about visual similarity feels too strong: The Abstract's inference from pseudo-to-real/real-to-pseudo asymmetry to visual similarity not being the primary cause is somewhat stronger than the design alone establishes. The asymmetry rules out a purely symmetric visual-confusability account and supports a substantial role for canonical-letter priors, but because the critical illusory response is also the mirrored, visually matched counterpart, visual similarity may still be an important enabling contributor to the errors.
issues.quote: Moreover, high confidence errors occurred mainly for pseudo-to-real letter memories, and much less often for real-to-pseudo-letter memories, indicating that visual similarity is not the primary cause of this memory-bias. Instead 'world knowledge' (e.g., which orientation letters usually have) appear to drive these STM illusions. Our findings support a predictive processing view of the formation and maintenance of memory in which all memory stages, including STM, involve integration of bottom-up memory input with top-down predictions, such that prior expectations can shape memory traces.

issues.subcategory: Overbroad claim about STM errors
issues.description: Overbroad claim about STM errors: The statement that failures to report recently presented information are “seldom interpreted as a memory error” is too broad for the STM/VWM context. The literature routinely treats short-delay reporting failures as memory errors due to capacity limits, precision loss, interference, or swaps. The intended point seems better limited to high-confidence qualitative illusions or brief-presentation paradigms in which such reports are often taken as evidence about perception rather than post-encoding reconstruction.
issues.quote: This illustrates the general assumption that STM is a highly reliable storage of recent events: failures to correctly report information that was only recently presented is seldom interpreted as a memory error, but usually seen as a perceptual error.

issues.subcategory: Inconsistent terminology (mirrored vs rotated)
issues.description: Inconsistent terminology (mirrored vs rotated): The passage shifts from “mirrored letters” to “the rotated letter” when referring to the same stimulus. Because reflection and rotation are distinct transformations in this context, this creates a local ambiguity about whether the cited stimuli were mirror-reversed, rotated, or whether the terms are being used interchangeably.
issues.quote: For example, De Gardelle and colleagues showed participants displays which sometimes contained mirrored letters (i.e., a pseudo-letter such as ()). The participants, however, often indicated seeing the real counterpart of the rotated letter (i.e., they report seeing C).

issues.subcategory: Confound between memory generation and decay
issues.description: Confound between memory generation and decay: Because the reported error rates are calculated within high-confidence trials, the temporal increase in illusory-error proportions may partly reflect changes in the high-confidence denominator rather than generation of new high-confidence illusions. If pseudo-letters that were initially encoded correctly lose high-confidence status faster than pseudo-letters initially misperceived or encoded as their familiar real counterparts, the proportion of high-confidence pseudo-to-real errors could rise even with a constant or declining absolute number of such errors. This leaves a differential-decay or survivorship alternative to the claim that the illusions necessarily arise during STM maintenance.
issues.quote: If the frequency of reported illusions increases over time, then at least part of the illusions can be attributed to memory processing rather than perceptual encoding. After all, at both time points initial perceptual processing was finished, so if the illusions arose completely during perception, they ought not to increase over time.

issues.subcategory: High-confidence criterion in the Introduction
issues.description: High-confidence criterion in the Introduction: The Introduction may overstate what high confidence establishes. High confidence is a useful criterion for excluding admitted low-confidence guesses, but it does not by itself distinguish an incorrect memory trace from confident inference, response bias, or metacognitive miscalibration, especially with highly familiar real-letter alternatives. The later delay and asymmetry analyses provide additional evidence, but the confidence filter is better treated as one converging indicator rather than as sufficient evidence of an actual false memory trace.
issues.quote:
Illusory memories should result in high confidence erroneous responses, where the participants has access to a memory trace (albeit an incorrect memory trace). In the absence of confidence ratings, the erroneous responses could actually consist of low confidence responses or even outright guesses. In these cases, the response is most likely not the result of an illusory memory. Instead, it is more likely to result from the absence of a reliable memory, which is compensated
by conscious inferences about what is likely to have occurred. Therefore, isolating high confidence responses is necessary to identify those responses that reflect a participant having an actual, albeit false, memory of perceiving something that was not there.

issues.subcategory: Temporal-increase rationale in the Introduction
issues.description: Temporal-increase rationale in the Introduction: The temporal-increase argument is somewhat too categorical. An increase in high-confidence illusory reports over delay is evidence against a simple account in which a fixed set of perceptual misperceptions is encoded and then reported unchanged, but it does not fully rule out perceptual or encoding contributions. Delay, interference, retrieval from degraded traces, and changes in confidence-based inclusion could all amplify an initially ambiguous or biased encoding.
issues.quote: To rule out that these errors reflect a perceptual error that has directly been encoded into STM, we test whether illusory responses increase over time: If the illusions are simply the result of misperceptions, their frequency of occurrence should remain the same over the time-course of STM - since in all cases initial perceptual inference has been completed. Moreover, we exclude the possibility that the errors are a result of guessing in the absence of reliable memories / reliable perception by focusing on high confidence errors: errors where the participant explicitly indicates to know the answer, and has not just guessed.

issues.subcategory: Confound in ruling out perceptual errors (Intro)
issues.description: Confound in ruling out perceptual errors (Intro): There seems to be a substantive denominator issue in the delay argument. The reported error rates appear to be conditional on high-confidence trials; if correct pseudo-letter representations lose confidence over delay faster than initially real-letter-like misperceptions do, the proportion of high-confidence pseudo-to-real errors could increase even if the absolute number of perceptually generated pseudo-to-real errors did not. This would make the temporal increase less decisive as evidence that new illusory memories are formed during STM maintenance, unless changes in high-confidence inclusion rates across delay and target type are ruled out or modelled.
issues.quote: To rule out that these errors reflect a perceptual error that has directly been encoded into STM, we test whether illusory responses increase over time: If the illusions are simply the result of misperceptions, their frequency of occurrence should remain the same over the time-course of STM - since in all cases initial perceptual inference has been completed.

issues.subcategory: Impossible stimulus dimensions in training task
issues.description: Impossible stimulus dimensions in training task: The reported training-stimulus dimensions, $0.05^{\circ} \times 0.01^{\circ}$, appear implausibly small for peripheral orientation discrimination at a radius of $4.68^{\circ}$. If taken literally, these rectangles would be only about 3 by 0.6 arcminutes, making it difficult to reconcile the method with the requirement that participants exceed 75% accuracy in training. This is likely a typographical error in the reported stimulus size and should be corrected for reproducibility.
issues.quote: The memory and test displays each consisted of eight white rectangles ( $0.05^{\circ} \times 0.01^{\circ}$ in size) which had horizontal, vertical or oblique ( $45^{\circ}$ or $135^{\circ}$ ) orientations.

issues.subcategory: Unaccounted participant attrition
issues.description: Unaccounted participant attrition: The Experiment 1 participant accounting is inconsistent. The Participants section says 40 participants remained after training, but the Analysis section reports an inclusion of 23 participants and says 5 participants were excluded for too few high-confidence critical trials. That accounts for only 28 of the 40 participants, leaving 12 participants unexplained. The paper should clarify the full participant flow and the final sample size used in the Experiment 1 analyses.
issues.quote: 45 participants started training, 5 participants were excluded based on their training results. The remaining 40 participants ( 28 female; age range 19-30 years, average age 22.2 years) all had normal or corrected-to-normal vision.

issues.subcategory: Experiment 1 timing makes the STM-report claim unclear
issues.description: Experiment 1 timing makes the STM-report claim unclear: The Experiment 1 timing would benefit from distinguishing more explicitly between the delay to the memory probe/cue and the delay to the overt identity response. As written, the Short condition probes the target location at 0.75 s, but the identity response is collected only after the irrelevant display at about 5 s after memory-display offset. This matters because some claims are phrased in terms of high-confidence reports occurring within 1–2 seconds, whereas Experiment 1 appears to operationalise the early condition as early cueing/probing rather than early overt report.
issues.quote: Figure 1 Experiment 1 - procedure. The memory display consisted of 6 or 8 letters. It contained 1 to 2 pseudo letters (set size 6) or 2 pseudo letters (set size 8). In all 3 memory delay conditions the trial started with the memory display appearing for 0.25 seconds. Subsequently in the Short and Long conditions (panel A) the memory cue appeared after a blank of 0.75 seconds (Short) or 3 seconds (Long), for 0.5 seconds, on a blank screen. Subsequently, 5 seconds after offset of the memory display, an irrelevant second letter display, containing the same amount of (randomly selected) real and pseudo-letters as the memory display, appeared for 0.5 seconds.

issues.subcategory: Contradictory confidence scales
issues.description: Contradictory confidence scales: The Figure 1 caption and the Experiment 1 Procedure section give contradictory confidence scales: the caption gives a 4-point scale (\$1=$ guess, \$4=$ certainty), whereas the Procedure section gives a 2-point scale (\$1=$ guess, \$2=$ certain). Since the Experiment 1 analyses are restricted to high-confidence trials, the paper should clarify the actual scale and the criterion used to classify a response as high confidence.
issues.quote: In all conditions, after offset of the second letter display, the participant first indicated the identity of the letter at the cued location in the memory display. Subsequently she indicated confidence in her judgment ( $1=$ guess, $4=$ certainty).

issues.subcategory: Experiment 1 counterpart trials may lack a correct target option
issues.description: Experiment 1 counterpart trials may lack a correct target option: The first sentence reads as if the exact target is always available, but the next paragraph says that on some trials the mirrored counterpart replaces it. Under the stated instruction to report the exact cued letter, those trials do not contain a correct exact-orientation option; the correct response would seem to be “none of these”. This matters because these are the trials used to define counterpart selections as memory illusions. Please state whether target-absent counterpart-only trials were included in the illusion analysis, excluded, or scored separately, and define the denominator used for the Experiment 1 error rates.
issues.quote:
The response display consisted of 6 letters: the target letter (with the same orientation as in the memory display, or mirror reversed), two other randomly selected letters from the memory display, and 3 letters that did not appear in the memory display.

The target letter was a real letter in $75 \%$ of the trials and a pseudo-letter in the remaining $25 \%$. If the target was a pseudo-letter, then it appeared as a response option randomly on half of those trials while on the other half of pseudo-letter trials only the real counterpart was one of the response options. If the target was a real letter, then it appeared as a response option on a randomly selected $83 \%$ of the trials, while its mirror reversed (pseudo-letter) version appeared as a response option on the other $16 \%$ of the trials.

issues.subcategory: Experiment 1 critical-trial percentages do not follow from the printed probabilities
issues.description: Experiment 1 critical-trial percentages do not follow from the printed probabilities: Using the percentages as printed, pseudo-to-real critical trials are 0.25 × 0.5 = 12.5% of all trials, while real-to-pseudo critical trials are 0.75 × 0.16 = 12.0%, for a total of 24.5%. This may be rounding, especially since 83% and 16% do not sum to 100%, but the paragraph should not leave readers guessing about the programmed trial list. Please report the exact programmed counts or exact probabilities behind the “~220 trials, 26%” statement.
issues.quote: The target letter was a real letter in $75 \%$ of the trials and a pseudo-letter in the remaining $25 \%$. If the target was a pseudo-letter, then it appeared as a response option randomly on half of those trials while on the other half of pseudo-letter trials only the real counterpart was one of the response options. If the target was a real letter, then it appeared as a response option on a randomly selected $83 \%$ of the trials, while its mirror reversed (pseudo-letter) version appeared as a response option on the other $16 \%$ of the trials. This ensured that of the critical trials (trials where participants could exhibit memory illusion: trials in which a real- or pseudo-letter target was combined with its mirrored counterpart in the response screen) about half were real-to-pseudo trials (approximately $13 \%$ of all trials), while the other half were pseudo-to-real trials (again, approximately $13 \%$ of all trials). Together, the critical trials made up $\sim 220$ trials, $26 \%$ of all trials in the experiment.

issues.subcategory: “None of these” responses are not classified in the analysis
issues.description: “None of these” responses are not classified in the analysis: The response options described in the procedure include “none of these”, but the analysis only defines illusory errors and unrelated-distractor errors. Readers need to know whether high-confidence “none” responses were counted as other errors, excluded, or analysed separately. This is especially important in Experiment 1, where the exact target could be absent from the response display on some trials.
issues.quote:
Participants were instructed to report the letter that appeared at the cued location. They were explicitly instructed not to confuse real and pseudo-letters and received feedback on their performance after each trial. They were instructed to select "none of these" if the target letter was not a response option. After selecting the target letter, participants indicated their confidence by clicking on one of two boxes (from 1-2, $1=$ guess, $2=$ certain).

Analysis
For each memory delay (short, short with interference and long) and each target type (pseudo- and real letter targets) the occurrence of illusory errors (real-to-pseudo or pseudo-to-real errors) and other errors (selection of one of the unrelated distractor items) was calculated.

issues.subcategory: Inconsistent participant exclusion numbers
issues.description: Inconsistent participant exclusion numbers: The Experiment 1 exclusion reporting is internally inconsistent. The Participants section says 40 participants completed the main experiment after training exclusions, but the Analysis says the high-confidence criterion resulted in 23 included participants while also stating that 5 participants were excluded. If 40 entered the main experiment and 23 were included, the corresponding exclusion count is 17, not 5.
issues.quote: Exclusion of participants with too few high confidence critical trials in one or more cells of the design (10 trials or less) were excluded from the analysis resulted in an inclusion of 23 participants ( 5 participants were excluded) when the results were averaged across the set size conditions.

issues.subcategory: Bayes-factor evidence labels are asymmetric around 1
issues.description: Bayes-factor evidence labels are asymmetric around 1: If Bayes factors above 1 favour inclusion or the alternative, the null-side labels should be reciprocal. A BF of 0.5 is the inverse of BF = 2, so it is only anecdotal evidence in the opposite direction, not substantial evidence. Likewise, BF < 0.33 corresponds to just over 3:1 evidence for the null, not the reciprocal of the usual >10 “strong” threshold. Revise the interpretation scale to use reciprocal ranges, for example 0.33–1 as anecdotal evidence for the null, 0.1–0.33 as substantial, and <0.1 as strong.
issues.quote: The resulting data were analysed in a Bayesian repeated measures ANOVA in JASP 0.16.4, with the factors Target Type (real or pseudo-letter), Memory Delay (short, short with interference and long) and Error Type. Within this analysis, the posterior odds of all different combinations the three factors and their interactions are compared to the prior explanatory value of each model. Based on this analysis, we selected the model with the best fit, reporting the BFm. Individual model components (main effects and interactions) were additionally evaluated based on their BFincl across all models. Bayes Factors were interpreted as follows: BF $<0.33$ : strong evidence for the null hypothesis. 0.33-1: substantial evidence for the null hypothesis. 1-3: anecdotal evidence for the alternative hypothesis, $3-10$ : substantial evidence for the alternative hypothesis, $>10$ : strong evidence for the alternative hypothesis

issues.subcategory: Directional hypotheses need planned contrasts, not only omnibus interactions
issues.description: Directional hypotheses need planned contrasts, not only omnibus interactions: The hypotheses are directional, but the listed ANOVA terms are not. A main effect of Error Type, and an Error Type × Memory Delay interaction, collapse across pseudo-to-real and real-to-pseudo errors; by themselves these effects show that mirrored-counterpart errors are more common, or increase more with delay, than other errors. They do not by themselves isolate the world-knowledge or expectation-specific component, which depends on effects involving Target Type. A Memory Delay × Error Type interaction can arise from several patterns, including a decrease in other errors with no increase in illusory errors. Likewise, a Target Type × Error Type interaction does not by itself show that pseudo-to-real errors exceed real-to-pseudo errors in the predicted way. Keep the omnibus tests if desired, but add the planned contrasts that match the claims: Short versus Long/Interference for illusory errors, and pseudo-to-real versus real-to-pseudo counterpart selections with the appropriate baseline.
issues.quote: We investigated our three main hypotheses: hypothesis 1 - do illusions occur in STM? - by determining if participants confused pseudo-letter targets with their real counterpart with high confidence, or the other way around, more often than other high confidence errors (main effect of Error Type). We tested our second hypothesis - do illusions increase as memory deteriorates? - by measuring if illusions increased from the Short to the other memory conditions (interaction between Memory Delay and Error Type). Finally, we tested our third hypothesis - does world knowledge drive STM illusions? - by investigating if high confidence errors confusing pseudo-letter targets for their real counterparts occurred more often than the other way around (Target Type interacts with Error Type).

issues.subcategory: Absolute differences are reported as percentage increases
issues.description: Absolute differences are reported as percentage increases: The reported changes are percentage-point differences, not relative percentage increases. For example, 26% − 19% = 7 percentage points; the relative increase would be about 37%. Similarly, 41% − 29% = 12 percentage points. Please use “percentage points” for these absolute differences throughout, otherwise the size comparisons can be misread.
issues.quote: The interaction between Error Type and Memory Delay, (BFincl = 4.21) shows support for hypothesis 2 : as memory deteriorates with a larger memory delay or more visual interference, the increase in illusory errors ( $7 \%$ increase from 19\% in the short delay to 26\% averaged over the short with interference and long delay) is larger than other errors ( $4 \%$ increase, from 8 to $12 \%$ ). The interaction between Target Type and Error Type (BFincl $>1000$ ) provides evidence for Hypothesis 3: when the target is a pseudo-letter, illusions are very common $(37 \%)$ but other errors occur much less often $(11 \%)$. For real letter targets, the illusory error rate is the same as the rate of erroneously selecting any other item from the response display ( $11 \%$ in both cases). Finally, there is only anecdotal evidence for a three-way interaction between Target Type, Error Type and Memory Delay (BFincl $=2.45$ ): For pseudo-letter targets, illusory errors increase $12 \%$ as memory deteriorates through interference of time or visual information ( $29 \%$ illusions to $41 \%$ illusions). None of the other conditions are as sensitive for memory decay, with other errors for pseudo-letter targets increasing 3\%, and illusory errors and other errors for real letter targets increasing 2\% and $7 \%$, respectively.

issues.subcategory: The Short-with-interference timing is misdescribed in the discussion
issues.description: The Short-with-interference timing is misdescribed in the discussion: The method says the Short-with-interference condition presented the second letter display together with the cue, not that the probe came after the interfering display. That distinction matters because simultaneous cueing and interference is a different manipulation from probing after interference has ended. Replace “when the probe was after an interfering visual display” with “when the probe was presented together with an interfering visual display”.
issues.quote: In Experiment 1 we observed an abundance of pseudo-to-real letter memory illusions. In fact, when the probe was after an interfering visual display, high confidence pseudo-to-real illusions ( $43 \%$ ) were almost as prevalent as high confidence selections of the actual pseudo-target $(50 \%)$.

issues.subcategory: The high- versus low-confidence comparison is not reported
issues.description: The high- versus low-confidence comparison is not reported: The analyses presented up to this point focus on high-confidence responses. They do not show the low-confidence denominator or a formal high- versus low-confidence comparison for the same illusion type. If this contrast is part of the argument, report the low-confidence illusion rates and the statistical test or Bayes factor. Otherwise, narrow the sentence to say that the present paper analyses high-confidence counterpart errors, without claiming that they are more frequent than their low-confidence counterparts.
issues.quote: This also shows that the current illusory memories are quite different from earlier reports of swap errors in STM , where participants incorrectly report having seen features of a distractor, instead of the target feature. While the currently observed memory illusions are more likely to occur in high confidence trials than on low confidence trials, swap errors generally occur on low confidence trials instead of high confidence trials.

issues.subcategory: Sampling of irrelevant display items needs an operational definition
issues.description: Sampling of irrelevant display items needs an operational definition: “Unrelated” is doing important work here. It could mean no exact glyph overlap, no shared base-letter identity, or no real/pseudo counterpart of any memory-display item. These cases are not equivalent: an intervening item sharing the target identity or its mirror counterpart could prime the very response later counted as an illusion. Please state the sampling rule for the second display, including whether both orientations of each memory-display identity were excluded.
issues.quote: The second, irrelevant, display also consisted of 4 real and 2 pseudo-letters. The letters in the second display were randomly selected and unrelated to the letters in the memory display.

issues.subcategory: Experiment 2 colour-by-target cell counts cannot be reconstructed
issues.description: Experiment 2 colour-by-target cell counts cannot be reconstructed: The conditional percentages do not specify the full trial structure. With 240 trials, the number of pseudo-letter targets is 0.25R + 0.60B, where R and B are the numbers of red and blue trials. Without the red/blue base rates, a reader cannot reconstruct the colour × target × delay cells or the number of observations behind the cue-colour test. Please give the planned counts per participant for each colour, target type, and delay condition.
issues.quote: If the fixation cross and the cue were red, a pseudo-letter was the target on $25 \%$ of the trials. The target was a pseudo-letter on $60 \%$ of the trials when the fixation cross and the cue were blue. Participants filled out a brief questionnaire in which they were invited to indicate what the experiment was about after the experiment. The relationship between the colour of the cue and the nature of the target was not mentioned in any of the responses. This experiment contained two memory delay conditions (short and long), two target types (real and pseudo) and two fixation color conditions (red and blue).

issues.subcategory: Cue-colour analysis omits memory delay
issues.description: Cue-colour analysis omits memory delay: The cue-colour null used to justify collapsing across colour appears to have been tested in a model that did not include memory delay. Because the paper’s account predicts stronger expectation effects as the memory trace deteriorates, this analysis does not rule out a delay-specific cue-colour effect on illusory errors.
issues.quote: First, we tested whether the cue colour influenced the occurrence of illusory errors, analysing the illusory error rates (real-to-pseudo or pseudo-to-real errors) in an ANOVA with target type (real or pseudo letter) and cue colour (red or blue, indicating low and high probability of a pseudoletter target) as factors. Since this analysis showed no effects of cue colour (see Results), the rest of the analysis was conducted while collapsing over the two cue colour conditions. As in Experiment 1, error rates on high confidence trials were analyzed in an ANOVA with target type (real or pseudo letter), memory delay (long or short) and error type (illusions -from pseudo-to-real or the other way around- vs other errors) as independent variables and relative occurrence of high confidence selection as the dependent variable.

issues.subcategory: Experiment 2 Analysis: cue-colour sample is ambiguous
issues.description: Experiment 2 Analysis: cue-colour sample is ambiguous: The Experiment 2 analysis is ambiguous about the sample used for the initial cue-colour ANOVA. The exclusion rule is reported only after the decision to collapse over cue colour and is qualified by “when the results were averaged across the two color conditions”, so it is not clear whether the cue-colour null result was based on the same 198 participants or on a different effective sample.
issues.quote: First, we tested whether the cue colour influenced the occurrence of illusory errors, analysing the illusory error rates (real-to-pseudo or pseudo-to-real errors) in an ANOVA with target type (real or pseudo letter) and cue colour (red or blue, indicating low and high probability of a pseudoletter target) as factors. Since this analysis showed no effects of cue colour (see Results), the rest of the analysis was conducted while collapsing over the two cue colour conditions. As in Experiment 1, error rates on high confidence trials were analyzed in an ANOVA with target type (real or pseudo letter), memory delay (long or short) and error type (illusions -from pseudo-to-real or the other way around- vs other errors) as independent variables and relative occurrence of high confidence selection as the dependent variable. Exclusion of participants with too few high confidence trials in one or more cells of the design ( 10 trials or less) resulted in an inclusion of 198 participants ( 92 participants were excluded) when the results were averaged across the two color conditions.

issues.subcategory: Collapsing over cue colour is not justified by the restricted preliminary model
issues.description: Collapsing over cue colour is not justified by the restricted preliminary model: The preliminary ANOVA only tests cue colour for illusory errors, crossed with target type. It does not test whether cue colour interacts with memory delay or whether it affects the “other error” category. Because the paper’s account predicts stronger expectation effects as the memory trace deteriorates, this analysis does not rule out a delay-specific cue-colour effect on illusory errors. A null result in this narrower analysis is not enough to justify collapsing before the full Target Type × Memory Delay × Error Type analysis. Please either report the full model including Cue Colour and all interactions needed for the later analysis, or make clear that the collapse is a simplifying choice rather than a result established by the stated test.
issues.quote: First, we tested whether the cue colour influenced the occurrence of illusory errors, analysing the illusory error rates (real-to-pseudo or pseudo-to-real errors) in an ANOVA with target type (real or pseudo letter) and cue colour (red or blue, indicating low and high probability of a pseudoletter target) as factors. Since this analysis showed no effects of cue colour (see Results), the rest of the analysis was conducted while collapsing over the two cue colour conditions.

issues.subcategory: The dependent variable is described in two different ways
issues.description: The dependent variable is described in two different ways: “Error rates on high confidence trials” and “relative occurrence of high confidence selection” are not the same quantity. The first asks, among high-confidence trials, how often each error type occurred. The second sounds like the probability that a given response was high-confidence. The hypotheses require the former. Please define the dependent variable as a proportion with numerator and denominator, for example: high-confidence illusory errors divided by all high-confidence critical trials in that cell.
issues.quote: As in Experiment 1, error rates on high confidence trials were analyzed in an ANOVA with target type (real or pseudo letter), memory delay (long or short) and error type (illusions -from pseudo-to-real or the other way around- vs other errors) as independent variables and relative occurrence of high confidence selection as the dependent variable.

issues.subcategory: Experiment 2 Analysis: high-confidence criterion unclear
issues.description: Experiment 2 Analysis: high-confidence criterion unclear: The Experiment 2 analysis does not specify how the 1–4 confidence scale was dichotomised for high-confidence trials. Because the exclusion of 92 participants and the reported high-confidence error rates depend on this threshold, the analysis is difficult to interpret or reproduce without knowing whether only the top rating, the upper part of the scale, or some other criterion was used.
issues.quote: Exclusion of participants with too few high confidence trials in one or more cells of the design ( 10 trials or less) resulted in an inclusion of 198 participants ( 92 participants were excluded) when the results were averaged across the two color conditions. Included participants had on average $49.2 \%$ high confidence trial over all conditions (range: $24.6-95.8$, sd: 13.3).

issues.subcategory: Confound in statistical criteria for Hypotheses 1 & 2
issues.description: Confound in statistical criteria for Hypotheses 1 & 2: The mapping between the ANOVA effects and the theoretical claims should be phrased more cautiously. A main effect of Error Type, and an Error Type × Memory Delay interaction, collapse across pseudo-to-real and real-to-pseudo errors; by themselves these effects show that mirrored-counterpart errors are more common, or increase more with delay, than other errors. They do not by themselves isolate the world-knowledge or expectation-specific component, which depends on effects involving Target Type.
issues.quote: Hypothesis 1 (Illusory memories occur in STM) would be supported if expectation-induced errors are more prevalent than other errors, resulting in a main effect of Error Type. Hypothesis 2 (These illusions are memory-driven) would be supported if high confidence illusory reports become more prevalent with longer memory delays, resulting in an interaction between Error Type and Memory Delay.

issues.subcategory: Experiment 2 Table 4 conflicts with the text
issues.description: Experiment 2 Table 4 conflicts with the text: In Experiment 2, the follow-up analysis for non-illusory errors appears internally inconsistent as printed. The prose reports that only Memory Delay was relevant, with $BF_{\mathrm{incl}} = 190$, and that Target Type did not affect these errors; Table 4 instead appears to list $BF_{\mathrm{incl}} = 0.064$ for Memory Delay and $BF_{\mathrm{incl}} = 39110.895$ for Target Type. The table or the prose therefore appears to be misreported.
issues.quote:
For other, non-illusory errors only Memory Delay was a relevant factor ( $\mathrm{BFm}=42$, see Appendix 1 for a full model comparison and Table 4 for an overview of BFincl for each model component). Non-illusory error rates increased from the short to the long delay (BFincl $=190$ for Memory Delay) but this increase was the same for pseudo- and real letter targets ( $2 \%$ increase, from 10 to $12 \%$, in both real and pseudo-letter targets).

issues.subcategory: General Discussion overstates the 500 ms timing
issues.description: General Discussion overstates the 500 ms timing: The General Discussion timing summary appears too specific for Experiment 1: its short probe was 0.75 s after memory-display offset, whereas 500 ms applies to Experiments 2 and 4. The broader claim about rapid formation is unaffected, but the cross-experiment timing statement should not group Experiment 1 under 500 ms.
issues.quote: Illusory memories make up almost $20 \%$ of reports when memory is probed at 500 ms (Experiment 1 and 2 ) and up to $30 \%$ of reports when memory is probed at 3 seconds (Experiment 1-4). Moreover, Experiments 3 and 4 show that pseudo-to-real letter illusory memories are also more prevalent than real-to-pseudo illusory memories when the stimulus set is completely balanced so that pseudo- and real letters occur equally often in the memory displays and as targets. Taken together, the results thus show that world knowledge can shape memory even when memories have only just been formed.

issues.subcategory: Weak-trace prediction in the General Discussion
issues.description: Weak-trace prediction in the General Discussion: The weak-trace argument appears to conflate item-level and category-level chance responding. If a lost pseudo-letter trace led participants to select all probe items with equal probability, the single mirrored counterpart would not generally be selected as often as the pooled category of other non-target options. The broader point that pseudo-to-real selections are selectively elevated may still hold, but the stated “similar rates” prediction is mathematically imprecise.
issues.quote: However, our findings clearly show that pseudo-letter targets do not simply lead to weaker memory traces. If that were the case, participants remembering a pseudo-letter target (or more accurately, a participant easily forgetting a weakly established representation of a pseudo-letter target) should be selecting all items in the probe display with equal probability, as the representation of the target has been lost. This should result in similar rates of errors (selecting probe items that are not the target, or a mirrored version of the target) and illusions (selecting the mirrored version of the target).

issues.subcategory: FTT similarity argument reverses its own prediction
issues.description: FTT similarity argument reverses its own prediction: The Fuzzy Trace Theory comparison contains a reversed entailment. If FTT is said to predict that high target–counterpart similarity should facilitate false memories, then the combination of extremely similar stimuli and abundant false memories is consistent with that stated prediction, not inconsistent with it. The intended tension may instead concern the asymmetry between pseudo-to-real and real-to-pseudo errors.
issues.quote: However, FTT predicts that high similarity between a target and its mirrored counterpart should facilitate false memories. This is not consistent with the current data: The mirrored counterpart (the real letter) and the target (the pseudo-letter) are extremely similar, yet false memories are abundant. Therefore, it seems that FTT cannot accurately account for the occurrence of this type of memory illusions in STM.

issues.subcategory: Conflation of "verbatim" and "verbal" representations
issues.description: Conflation of "verbatim" and "verbal" representations: The discussion appears to shift from FTT’s “verbatim” trace to verbal or phonological rehearsal. Verbatim traces in FTT are exact representations of the input and need not be verbal; in this task they would plausibly include visual form and orientation. Unless this is meant as a separate working-memory maintenance account, attributing the verbal-rehearsal claim to FTT risks mischaracterising the theory.
issues.quote: FTT does suggest that pseudo-letters have a verbal (the letter itself) and a gist level ("mirrored") representation, while real letters can be stored purely at the verbal level. This would mean that verbal rehearsal is more effective to store a complete representation of real letters in working memory, but not for pseudo-letters.

issues.subcategory: Overgeneralisation to all STM stages
issues.description: Overgeneralisation to all STM stages: The transition overstates the scope of the evidence. The paper first says that the experiments do not test whether illusory memories arise in iconic memory, but then presents susceptibility across “all stages of STM” as a fact. The supported claim is narrower: the experiments provide evidence for illusory memories in working memory and fragile memory, while iconic memory remains untested here.
issues.quote:
Our experiments currently do not test whether illusory memories arise in IM, which is sometimes thought not to be susceptible to illusions based on contextual information or internally generated biases .

The implications of STM illusory memories for vision research
The fact that all stages of STM are susceptible to illusory memories has important implications for vision research, as WM and IM tasks are often used to investigate the content of the visual percept for example in visual masking tasks or in change blindness tasks.

issues.subcategory: Contradiction regarding initial memory trace
issues.description: Contradiction regarding initial memory trace: The phrase that memory is shaped by expectations “right from the formation of the first memory trace” could be read as in tension with the paper’s earlier account that participants mainly begin with a correct percept and that encoded pseudo-letter percepts are later converted into real-letter memories. The evidence supports a rapid post-offset influence of expectations that strengthens as the trace degrades; it does not by itself show that the initial STM trace is already distorted at formation.
issues.quote: Thus, it seems that short-term memory is not always an accurate representation of what was just perceived. Instead, memory is shaped by what we expected to see, right from the formation of the first memory trace.
